title: Rank critical assets by what they make possible
goal: You can say which critical assets matter most and why, in one page.
steps: List the critical assets you are reporting. | Score each on reuse value, the outcomes it supports, the people affected and the risk if it fails, using the scorecard. | Note where legacy systems, poor quality or missing ownership hold an asset back. | Agree the top ten with the data governance board and record the decision.
outputs: Prioritisation scorecard | Board decision on the top ten
evidence: The board's decision log records the ranking and the reasons.
measure: Share of critical assets scored.

title: Put the ranking into the data strategy
goal: The data strategy names the assets it depends on and the outcomes they serve.
steps: Link each strategic objective to the critical assets it needs. | Set a target for each top asset, such as owner in post, metadata complete or quality in range. | Publish the ranking method with the strategy so teams can apply it to new assets.
outputs: Data strategy with named assets and targets
evidence: The strategy names critical assets and targets for them.
measure: Strategic objectives that name the assets they depend on.

title: Re-rank every year with the return
goal: Priorities follow what changed, not what was decided once.
steps: Re-score assets during the annual review, using the same scorecard. | Show what moved up or down and why. | Feed the changes into investment and business planning.
evidence: Each year's ranking is kept with the reasons for changes.
measure: Years with a re-ranking on record.

title: Map the tools you have against what the policy needs
goal: You know which capabilities your tools cover, which they miss and when contracts end.
steps: List the tools used for cataloguing, quality, lineage, master data, governance workflow and records. | Record the owner, contract end date and how each connects to the others. | Mark each against the functional requirements for its kind of tool, Musts first. | Note gaps the next return would expose.
evidence: Each tool has an owner, a contract end date and a gap assessment.
measure: Tools assessed against the Must requirements.

title: Run a request for information with ready-made requirements
goal: Suppliers answer the same questions, so answers can be compared.
steps: Choose the kinds of tool you need and copy their requirements into the schedule. | Change priorities to suit, and agree them with your commercial team. | Publish the RFI through your usual route, and search Find a Tender and G-Cloud for how others specified similar tools. | Score the answers, then shortlist for a proof of concept.
evidence: Every response is scored against the same requirements.
measure: Requirements answered with evidence.

title: Prove it with your own data before you sign
goal: The tool does what the supplier says, with your data and your other tools.
steps: Load test copies of two of your critical assets. | Export everything and import it into another product or an empty instance; record what is lost. | Show quality results in the catalogue through an open route, and capture lineage from a pipeline you own. | Score each requirement on what you saw.
outputs: Proof of concept test log | Evaluation scores
evidence: A test log with a result for every Must.
measure: Must requirements proved, not only claimed.

title: Check before every renewal
goal: You can still leave, and the tool still meets the policy.
steps: Repeat the full export test each year before renewal. | Re-score the Must requirements, and record any that have slipped. | Decide to renew, renegotiate or replace, and record the decision.
evidence: An export test and a decision before each renewal.
measure: Renewals with an export test on record.

title: Record the main risk to each critical asset
goal: Every critical asset has at least one risk on a register someone reviews.
steps: For each critical asset, ask what would happen if it was unavailable, wrong, exposed or not kept. | Record the worst credible risk on the corporate or programme risk register, with the owner as risk owner. | Score it with your organisation's risk method, and link it to the asset's catalogue record.
evidence: Each critical asset has a linked risk with an owner.
measure: Critical assets with a recorded risk.

title: Set risk appetite for data
goal: Owners know how much risk they can accept and when to escalate.
steps: Agree a risk appetite statement for data with the board, for availability, accuracy, privacy and retention. | Set escalation thresholds and who they go to. | Use exceptions, with an expiry date, for risks accepted outside appetite.
evidence: The board has approved a data risk appetite.
measure: Risks outside appetite with an action or a dated exception.

title: Review data risks with the asset review
goal: Risks stay current as assets and systems change.
steps: Review each asset's risks in its annual review. | Close risks that have gone and add new ones from quality issues, incidents and audits. | Report the top data risks to the board each quarter.
evidence: Each risk shows a review date in the last year.
measure: Data risks reviewed in the last 12 months.

title: Find the critical assets held or supplied by third parties
goal: You know which critical assets depend on a supplier, and on which contract.
steps: For each critical asset, record any supplier that holds, processes or provides it. | Name the contract, its end date and whether it covers data ownership, processing and return. | Mark gaps for the next renewal.
evidence: Every critical asset held by a supplier names the contract.
measure: Supplier-held critical assets with ownership and return covered in the contract.

title: Put data terms in every new contract
goal: New contracts protect critical data from the start.
steps: Use the contract clauses on the Tools and interoperability page as a checklist. | Include a data processing schedule wherever personal data is processed. | Require metadata to be supplied with the data, in the government format.
evidence: New contracts that touch critical assets include the clauses.
measure: New contracts with the data clauses.

title: Test the return of data before contracts end
goal: Data comes back complete when a contract ends.
steps: A year before a contract ends, ask for a test return of the data and its metadata. | Check completeness and format against what the contract says. | Fix gaps before the exit, not after.
evidence: A test return before each relevant contract ends.
measure: Contracts ending with a successful test return.

title: Check what each data role needs to know
goal: Everyone named in a data role knows what is expected of them.
steps: List everyone named as owner, steward, custodian or catalogue manager. | Ask each to rate themselves against the learning outcomes for their role on the Learning page. | Point each to the modules that close their gaps.
outputs: Skills assessment | Learning plan per person
evidence: Every named role holder has a learning plan.
measure: Named role holders who have completed their core modules.

title: Build data roles into jobs and objectives
goal: Data roles are part of the job, not extra to it.
steps: Add data ownership and stewardship to job descriptions and objectives where they apply. | Map specialist roles to the Digital and Data Capability Framework. | Give time for the role, and recognise it in performance reviews.
evidence: Named role holders have the role in their objectives.
measure: Role holders with the role in their objectives.

title: Keep a community of practice going
goal: People in data roles learn from each other, inside and across organisations.
steps: Run a regular session for owners and stewards to share problems and fixes. | Join the cross-government data management community and its boards. | Induct new role holders within a month of appointment.
outputs: Community sessions | Induction for new role holders
evidence: New role holders are inducted within a month.
measure: Days from appointment to induction.

title: Find out who uses each critical asset and what gets in their way
goal: Owners know their users and their main problems.
steps: For each top critical asset, list the teams and services that use it. | Ask a few users what stops them using it well, and record the answers. | Feed the main problems into the quality plan and the catalogue record.
outputs: User list and problems per asset
evidence: Top critical assets have a list of users and their problems.
measure: Top assets with user feedback in the last year.

title: Tell people what changed because of their feedback
goal: Users see that raising a problem leads to a fix.
steps: Publish a short note each quarter on what was fixed and what is planned. | Name the owner and the way to raise new problems. | Include the people the data describes where the asset is about them.
evidence: A note published each quarter.
measure: Problems raised that have a response.

title: Make data work visible to leaders
goal: Leaders ask about data assets as they ask about money and people.
steps: Report the state of critical assets to the executive board with other corporate measures. | Include one story a quarter of a decision or service improved by better data. | Thank people in data roles publicly.
evidence: Critical assets appear in executive reporting.
measure: Executive board meetings that discuss data assets.

title: Take a baseline
goal: You know your starting level for each strand of data asset management.
steps: Use the self-assessment on the Capability model page for a first view. | Where you can, run the Data Maturity Assessment for Government with the people who do the work. | Record the level for each strand, with the evidence for it.
evidence: A baseline with evidence for each level.
measure: Strands with an evidenced baseline.

title: Set targets and an improvement plan
goal: Each strand has a target level, a date and the actions to reach it.
steps: Set a target level for each strand, starting with the level the DAM Policy needs for critical assets. | Choose the actions from the playbooks that move each strand up. | Agree owners and dates with the board.
evidence: The board has approved targets and a plan.
measure: Plan actions on track.

title: Reassess every year
goal: Progress is measured, not assumed.
steps: Repeat the assessment each year, with the same method. | Compare with the baseline and explain changes. | Reset targets and actions.
evidence: An assessment each year with evidence.
measure: Strands that moved up a level.

title: Name the critical assets in every business case
goal: Business cases say which critical assets they create, change or depend on.
steps: Add a data assets section to your business case template. | For each asset, state its owner, its catalogue record and what the change does to it. | Ask for this at the first approval point.
outputs: Data assets section in business cases
evidence: Business cases list the critical assets they affect.
measure: Business cases approved with the section completed.

title: Make the case for investing in data assets
goal: Investment in data assets is argued with costs, benefits and the cost of doing nothing.
steps: Use the five cases of the Green Book business case structure. | Count the cost of the current state, such as manual cleansing, duplicate collection and failed sharing. | Show benefits as measures you will track, with an owner for each.
evidence: A business case with measurable benefits and owners.
measure: Benefits with an owner and a baseline.

title: Fund the yearly cycle in business as usual
goal: The annual review, catalogue and quality work have a budget that does not end with a project.
steps: Cost the yearly cycle: reviews, catalogue upkeep, quality checks and the return. | Put it in the business-as-usual budget of the teams that own the assets. | Review the cost each year with the ranking of assets.
evidence: A budget line for the yearly cycle.
measure: Owning teams with a budget for the cycle.

title: Add data asset questions to existing checkpoints
goal: Spend control, gate reviews and service assessments ask about critical data.
steps: Add three questions to internal spend control and gate review templates. | Agree with the assessment team that service assessments will look for the evidence. | Brief programme managers on what good evidence looks like.
evidence: Checkpoint templates include the questions.
measure: Checkpoints that asked the questions this year.

title: Put data checkpoints into the assurance plan
goal: Large programmes plan their data assurance from the start.
steps: Add data asset checkpoints to the integrated assurance and approval plan. | Name who gives the assurance and what evidence they need. | Record findings and actions with the other assurance findings.
evidence: Major programmes have data checkpoints in their assurance plans.
measure: Programmes with data checkpoints planned.

title: Learn from checkpoint findings
goal: Common problems are fixed in guidance, not found again and again.
steps: Collect findings about data assets from all checkpoints each quarter. | Spot repeated problems and fix the guidance or templates. | Share the lessons with programme managers.
evidence: A quarterly summary of findings and fixes.
measure: Repeated findings falling over time.

title: List the critical assets in each legacy system
goal: You know what data each legacy system holds before anyone plans to replace it.
steps: For each system with a planned end, list the critical assets it holds or feeds. | Record what depends on them downstream. | Mark data that must be kept for records or legal reasons.
evidence: Each system with a planned end has its assets listed.
measure: Legacy systems with an asset register.

title: Migrate with reconciliation
goal: Data arrives complete and correct, and you can prove it.
steps: Agree mapping and transformation rules with the owner before migration. | Reconcile counts, totals and samples between old and new, and record differences. | Fix or accept differences, with the owner's decision recorded.
evidence: A signed-off reconciliation for each migrated asset.
measure: Migrated assets with a signed-off reconciliation.

title: Switch off safely
goal: Nothing needed is lost when a system is turned off.
steps: Check every asset on the register is migrated, archived or disposed of under the schedule. | Update the catalogue records, marking retired assets and what replaced them. | Get the owner's sign-off before switch-off.
evidence: The owner signs off before switch-off.
measure: Switch-offs with owner sign-off.

title: Name the business-as-usual owner early
goal: Every asset a project creates has an owner who will be there after the project.
steps: At the start of delivery, name the business-as-usual owner and steward for each new asset. | Involve them in design decisions about the data. | Record them in the catalogue from the first release.
evidence: New assets have a business-as-usual owner in the catalogue.
measure: New assets with a named business-as-usual owner.

title: Hand over with a checklist
goal: Business as usual receives everything needed to run the asset.
steps: Use the handover checklist: owner, steward, catalogue record, quality plan, risks, contracts, documentation and budget. | Walk through it with the receiving owner. | Do not close the project until the owner signs.
evidence: A signed checklist for each asset.
measure: Projects closed with signed handovers.

title: Check six months after handover
goal: The asset is still owned, catalogued and checked after the project team has gone.
steps: Six months after handover, check the owner, catalogue record and quality plan are current. | Record and fix any gaps. | Share lessons with the programme office.
evidence: A check six months after each handover.
measure: Handovers still complete at six months.

title: Pick a few measures and record the baseline
goal: You can show change, because you know where you started.
steps: Choose three to five measures, such as reuse requests met, duplicate collections stopped or time spent cleansing. | Record today's value for each, and how you measured it. | Name an owner for each benefit.
evidence: Each measure has a baseline and an owner.
measure: Benefits with a recorded baseline.

title: Track and report the benefits
goal: Leaders see progress against the baseline each quarter.
steps: Measure each benefit on its schedule, the same way as the baseline. | Report progress to the board with the other data measures. | Explain changes, including those not caused by the work.
evidence: Benefits reported each quarter against the baseline.
measure: Benefits on track.

title: Evaluate after a year
goal: You know what worked, what did not and why.
steps: Plan a proportionate evaluation using the Magenta Book. | Compare results with the business case. | Publish the lessons for other organisations.
evidence: An evaluation within a year of the main change.
measure: Lessons published.

title: Ask three questions of every new system
goal: No new system holds critical data you cannot get out.
steps: Ask whether the data can be exported in full, in an open format, with a published schema. | Ask whether the export has been tested. | Ask what leaving would cost and how long it would take.
evidence: Design reviews record the three answers.
measure: New systems with recorded answers.

title: Write and cost the exit plan
goal: Leaving is planned and costed before you sign.
steps: Write an exit plan for each system holding critical data, with the formats, steps and time it would take. | Cost it and put the cost in the business case. | Put the plan in the contract.
evidence: Systems holding critical data have a costed exit plan.
measure: Systems with a costed exit plan.

title: Test the exit every year
goal: The exit plan still works.
steps: Run a full export each year and check it against the plan. | Record anything lost or changed. | Update the plan and raise any gap with the supplier.
evidence: An exit test each year.
measure: Systems with an exit test in the last year.
